From the hardware/software perspective, VGA supports 262,144 colors. It introduces the concept of a palette, where the value associated with each pixel isn't a color, but a reference to a "slot" (or entry) on a palette. Each palette slot can be defined to 6 bits red, 6 bits green, 6 bits blue = 18 bits = 262,144 different colors. There are only 256 entries in the palette table (so 256 slots), and thus only 256 different colors can be shown at one time.

USB-C is the physical form factor. The numbered name (e.g. USB 3.1) is the signaling. So USB 1.0, USB 2.0, and the former USB 3.0 can all run over USB-A/USB-B, and over USB-C (on the legacy/signaling lines). USB 3.1 and USB 3.2 (and whatever they're renamed to) can only run over USB-C. There are also mini/micro versions of USB-A and USB-B, and mini and micro (but not full sized) forms of USB-AB (for devices that can act as both a host and a client).

USB-C is great because it's not end-oriented (i.e. the cables are identical on each end and it doesn't matter which end you use, with one exception), it's almost as small as the micro versions of legacy USB connectors, and it's completely backwards compatible with both the physical form factor and allowed signaling (though the standard only allows cables with USB-B on one end and USB-C on the other, because of potential damaging electrical paths that could be made by connecting a legacy host to a legacy host with passive form factor converters). So yeah, USB-C is super and everything should move to using it (that is, if you ignore the cost of replacing existing devices and the hassle of getting manufacturers to start using it).

Here's how it happened: VGA only had a finite amount of analog bandwidth. Higher and higher resolutions would benefit from a digital standard, so one was created: DVI.

But it had to be backward compatible with analog, or it wouldn't be accepted and people would scream bloody murder, so it was very large and had redundant pins for analog and digital. This, DVI-D and DVI-I were designated to distinguish between pure digital connections and ones that also supported analog (and could therefore be easily converted to VGA).

Also, the movie cartels were scared of raw, unencrypted digital connections so they demanded a new standard with compulsory built in security. While DVI supported HDCP security as an option, it was built into the HDMI standard. HDMI also included a smaller, more convenient plug size while maintaining pin-for-pin backwards compatibility with DVI.

Now, HDMI was a standard that required a license fee to be paid for every device and plug that contained an HDMI connector. HP and some other tech companies weren't happy with that, so the DisplayPort digital standard was born. This was an open standard that could be used freely. DisplayPort is also compatible with HDMI, but only in one direction. A video output device with a DisplayPort connection can connect to a display with an HDMI port with a simple cable with the correct plugs on both ends.

You cannot connect in the other direction, however. As HDMI does not convert cleanly to DisplayPort inputs but this is very rarely an issues that comes up since most displays all have HDMI while very few only have DisplayPort.

The "mini" versions of the same were born out of necessity. Smaller devices like ultrabooks, smartphones, and tablets didn't have room for full-size connections, so the same standards were shrunk down to fit mobile units.

While it may all seem very confusing, just buy cables with the right ends and generally things will just work.
